title: Mars Tracker
narrative: Where things stand on 31 October 2026. Two NASA rovers are working on the surface: Curiosity and Perseverance. Perseverance set a new distance record on 11 October (45.22 km, past the 45.16 km that NASA's Opportunity rover drove), and on 24 October it drilled its first new rock sample in more than a year, "Singita", which the team says may be among the oldest rocks exposed on Mars. Curiosity is getting ready to drill a new hole at a rock called "Nazca". Japan's Martian Moons eXploration probe (MMX) launched on 20 October and is on its way; JAXA says its critical first days in space are done and the spacecraft is healthy; on 30 October the French space agency CNES woke the small Idefix rover riding on MMX for a planned test, which went well. Arrival at Mars is August 2027 per ESA, NASA and NASASpaceFlight; JAXA's press kit gives only "fiscal year 2027" (April 2027 to March 2028). NASA published (26 October) the first measurements on Mars of the very fine dust that future crews would have to deal with. NASA's four-person, yearlong Mars simulation on Earth (CHAPEA) ends today, 31 October, with the crew leaving the habitat at 21:00 Israel time. New on 29 October: a NASA-funded study in the journal Science dates a meteorite from Mars found in the Sahara, "Teghaza 001", to more than 4.1 billion years ago, making it one of the oldest pieces of Mars known.

Budget and Congress: a stopgap funding law keeps NASA at its 2026 level of $24.4 billion through 11 December 2026. The White House asked for $18.8 billion for 2027, and the House committee bill kept NASA flat at $24.4 billion. Mars Sample Return (bringing Perseverance's rock tubes to Earth) was cancelled and has no replacement plan. Two bid protests (formal challenges to a contract award) are now open at the Government Accountability Office (GAO) against NASA's Mars Telecommunications Network award to Blue Origin; the second was filed on 23 October.

Plans from companies and agencies are goals, not funded schedules, unless the entry says otherwise. They are marked [aspirational]. Facts I could not match to a second source are marked [unconfirmed]. A sol is one Martian day, about 24 hours 39 minutes.

feed.who: CNES (France's space agency), post on X
feed.kind: primary source (CNES built and runs the Idefix rover with Germany's DLR)
feed.text: Engineers at CNES's control center in Toulouse woke up Idefix, the small French-German rover riding on Japan's MMX spacecraft, and the planned test sequence went well, CNES says. CNES puts MMX at more than 3 million km from Earth and says the next wake-up is in a month. Idefix is meant to be set down on Phobos, the larger moon of Mars, to drive on its surface; it stays attached to MMX until then.
feed.evidence: CNES's own post (in French; translated here). No CNES or DLR web page about the wake-up found yet, and the 3 million km figure has no second source [unconfirmed]

feed.who: NASA, news release 2026-079, "NASA-funded Study Details One of Oldest Mars Meteorites Ever Found"
feed.where: nasa.gov (posted 2:18 p.m. U.S. Eastern time, 20:18 Israel time)
feed.text: A rose-colored meteorite (a rock that fell to Earth from space) found in the Sahara in Mali in 2022, named Teghaza 001, formed on Mars more than 4.1 billion years ago, according to a study published 29 October in the journal Science. That makes it one of the three oldest of the roughly 435 Martian meteorites known; the others are ALH84001, found in Antarctica in 1984, which is of similar age, and "Black Beauty". Water altered the rock about 4.1 billion years ago, so it formed even earlier, and the team says this supports the idea that early Mars had liquid water and conditions that could have suited life, though it does not show that life existed. It is a single kind of coarse igneous rock (gabbro, which cooled slowly from molten rock below the surface), unlike Black Beauty, which is a jumble of many rock pieces. Its minerals best match Mars's ancient southern highlands as seen from orbit by NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO); NASA shows 13 possible source spots on a MOLA map (an elevation map made by a laser altimeter on the old Mars Global Surveyor orbiter). The lead author is Yang Liu of JPL; the University of New Mexico first spotted that it came from Mars from its oxygen isotopes (different forms of the oxygen atom).
feed.evidence: official NASA release about a peer-reviewed paper; the main facts (found in Mali in 2022, at least 4.1 billion years old, about 435 Martian meteorites, lead author Liu) match Reuters (Will Dunham, 29 Oct) and the University of New Mexico's own release. I did not open the Science paper itself (the journal site refused my reader)
feed.other: The sources describe the dating a little differently: NASA names rubidium-strontium dating of mineral grains, while Reuters and the University of New Mexico describe uranium-lead dating of tiny zircon crystals; the paper may use both [unconfirmed]. Reuters reports the rock was found in eight pieces about 34 km (21 miles) from the village of Bir Chali, and quotes Liu that it may come from near the Hellas Basin, a huge impact crater. NASA puts it at about 800 grams (nearly 2 pounds) [unconfirmed by a second source]. The University of New Mexico is a partner in the study (an interested source). @NASAMars posted the story on X at 22:10 Israel time.
links: NASA map of possible source spots (Photojournal)
NASA photo of a slice of the meteorite (Photojournal)
University of New Mexico release (study partner)

feed.who: Asa Stahl, The Planetary Society (a space advocacy group), "Mars rover samples what could be one of the oldest rocks on the Martian surface"
feed.image_alt: A round, glowing view down into a tube, with a pale disc inside a bright ring, on a dark brown background
feed.image_caption: Raw image from Perseverance's sample-caching camera (CacheCam), which looks into sample tubes inside the rover, sol 2018 (24 October 2026). This is the day the Planetary Society says Singita was drilled; NASA's raw-image feed does not name the sample, so I cannot confirm this frame shows Singita. Raw image, not processed or checked
feed.image_credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech, NASA raw image (generally not copyrighted), from NASA's public raw-image feed
feed.kind: advocacy group (interested source), reporting a NASA team announcement
feed.text: For the first time in more than a year, Perseverance has collected a rock sample. On 24 October it drilled a core called "Singita" in the "Lac de Charmes" region outside the western rim of Jezero crater. The news was first given by Katie Stack Morgan, the mission's project scientist, at the American Astronomical Society's planetary sciences meeting (the Division for Planetary Sciences, DPS). She said it "could be among the oldest rocks exposed on the surface of Mars". Jezero itself formed about 3.9 billion years ago, and Singita, a crystalline igneous rock (one that cooled from molten rock), could be several hundred million years older. It was probably buried about 1 km deep before an impact threw it up to the surface; it may even be a piece of the impact that made the giant Isidis basin. Only lab work on Earth could give its exact age. The rock was so hard that the first try failed, and the rover switched to a less-used drill bit. Stack Morgan said the rover will stay in the area to try for two more samples, one of them from a younger igneous rock.
feed.evidence: the Planetary Society's report of a talk by NASA's project scientist; NASA had not posted its own story when I checked on 29 October. NASA's raw-image feed does show sample-camera (CacheCam) pictures taken on sol 2018 (24 October), which fits a sample being taken that day. The age is the team's estimate, not a measurement
feed.other: NASA's 5 October team blog "A Journey to the Depths of Ancient Mars?" describes the light-toned gabbro boulders (a coarse igneous rock from deep in the crust) in Lac de Charmes and a possible breccia at "Idubi" that may be their source. NASA's 12 October count of 29 rock and regolith samples was before Singita.
links: Planetary Society image page (CacheCam photo of the core)

feed.who: NASA Curiosity team blog, sols 5043-5049, "Preparing to Drill at 'Nazca'", by Lucy Lim (planetary scientist, NASA Goddard)
feed.text: After the "Basque Lakes" drill campaign, Curiosity drove back near the "Chiu Chiu" block and is preparing to drill at "Nazca", a neighboring block packed with disc- and needle-shaped shapes that may be crystals, or pseudomorphs (minerals that have replaced earlier crystals but kept their shape). The plan for the week: a drill "preload" test (pressing the drill on the rock without drilling, to check it is safe), a 3D model of Nazca's surface from five overlapping close-up camera (MAHLI) pictures, laser shots by ChemCam (an instrument that zaps rock with a laser and reads the light to learn its chemistry) on targets "Toucan", Nazca and the finely layered "Condor", dust brushing and an X-ray chemistry reading (APXS) on Nazca, and night pictures of a full Phobos to estimate the size of particles in high, thin carbon-dioxide clouds; the twilight cloud season is starting. The plan was made on 16 October; the post's picture is from sol 5048 (18 October 2026).
feed.evidence: official NASA blog, named author; no new drill hole is reported yet (NASA's mission page still counts 42)

feed.who: CNSPACE (@CNSpaceflight), a Chinese spaceflight news account on X (not an agency), passing on a post by @Rain_Antar1121
feed.text: Rumor, not an announcement: two X accounts say China may split its Tianwen-3 Mars sample-return mission. The orbiter-and-return spacecraft would still launch in November 2028 to scout landing sites from orbit, but the lander and the small rocket that would lift samples off Mars (the Mars Ascent Vehicle) are behind schedule and could wait for the next launch window two years later. That would move the samples' arrival on Earth from about 2031 to about 2033. The original poster says an unnamed industry contact told them the plan was issued only weeks ago and is still being discussed. China has said nothing about this [unconfirmed]. China's last public plan (Xinhua, April 2026) was launch about 2028 and samples back about 2031.
feed.evidence: anonymous source passed on by two X accounts; no Chinese agency or state media page says this; I searched and found nothing that confirms it
feed.other: The original Chinese post says the picture it carries is unrelated and shows the old plan.

feed.who: Ling Xin, South China Morning Post (a Hong Kong newspaper), on a paper by Zhang Zhe and colleagues
feed.kind: named reporter (secondary source), with the paper's abstract read
feed.where: scmp.com and the Journal of Deep Space Exploration
feed.text: A team at the state-funded Deep Space Exploration Laboratory in Hefei, China, reports a lab catalyst (a material that speeds up a chemical reaction) that turns carbon dioxide, which makes up more than 95 percent of Mars's air, plus hydrogen into methanol, a liquid fuel. This is the kind of ISRU (making fuel or air from what is already on Mars) that future crews would need. The paper's abstract says the best version, called MOF-808-NaCu (copper and sodium held in a porous framework), made 245 grams of methanol per kilogram of catalyst per hour, about 11 times the 22 grams of the same material without sodium, and made less carbon monoxide waste. The paper was published online in China's Journal of Deep Space Exploration.
feed.evidence: the paper's own abstract (Chinese journal page) and a newspaper report; laboratory work on Earth, not a test on Mars, and the hydrogen would also have to be made on Mars
feed.link_text: open the paper's page (Chinese and English abstract)
feed.other: The SCMP article is dated 27 October 2026 (12:00 p.m. Hong Kong time, 06:00 Israel time).

feed.who: NASA, media advisory M26-083 (Lauren E. Low), "NASA Invites Media to Crew Completion of Yearlong Mars Simulation"
feed.image_alt: Four people in black flight suits posing in front of a red, Mars-like backdrop with sand on the floor
feed.image_caption: The CHAPEA Mission 2 crew (from left) Ross Elder, Matthew Montgomery, Ellen Ellis and James Spicer, photographed on 8 October 2025, before they went in. A posed photo on Earth, not on Mars
feed.text: Four volunteers who have lived for more than a year in a pretend Mars base on Earth come out on Saturday, 31 October, after 378 days. The mission is CHAPEA (Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog), its second run; it began on 19 October 2025 in a 3D-printed, 1,700-square-foot building at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston. The crew did simulated spacewalks, grew plants and fixed the habitat while living with message delays, limited supplies and isolation, the way a real Mars crew would. NASA will stream the exit live from 3 p.m. EDT (21:00 Israel time). NASA now says the data will mainly help its Moon missions (Artemis and a Moon base).
feed.evidence: official NASA advisory; @NASAJohnson posted the same date on 27 October

feed.who: Scholar (Grok Bot research agent) for you
feed.text: Scholar's Mars exploration course is published: how Mars has been explored, a map set, where each mission stands, and what is planned. Its facts were checked on 27 October 2026 and carry its own labels, [unconfirmed] and [aspirational], which this page keeps. This tracker starts from the course and re-checked its time-sensitive items against NASA, JAXA, GAO, ESA, UAE and Xinhua pages today. Where the course and a primary source differ, this page follows the primary source and says so (for example: the Xinhua interview with Tianwen-3's chief scientist is dated 3 September, not 4 September; and a second GAO protest exists).

feed.who: NASA Mars (@NASAMars), official NASA account
feed.text: Posts that scientists are using instruments on Perseverance to study the dust on Mars and how it could harm future crews and equipment (the post's subject is the dust study NASA also lists on the Perseverance mission page).
feed.evidence: official NASA account; the linked JPL copy of the article gave my reader an access error (403), but NASA's copy on nasa.gov opened on 28 October (see the 26 October NASA release item)
feed.other: The JPL copy, which gave an access error before, opened on 29 October. NASA's Perseverance mission page lists the story under the headline "NASA's Perseverance Offers Clues to Protect Crews From Mars Dust".

feed.who: NASA, news release 2026-076, "NASA's Perseverance Offers Clues to Protect Crews From Mars Dust"
feed.image_alt: Wide view of a rocky, dusty Martian channel with low hills; part of the rover's deck shows at the right edge
feed.image_caption: File picture, not new: a 360-degree enhanced-color view of Neretva Vallis that Perseverance's Mastcam-Z camera took on 20 May 2024 (sol 1155), stitched from 217 images. Enhanced color makes differences in the ground easier to see; it is not what the eye would see
feed.image_credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU/MSSS, NASA image (generally not copyrighted), NASA Photojournal PIA26816
feed.text: Over 1,645 sols (Martian days), Perseverance measured how much very fine dust settled on small squares of spacesuit material it carries: Teflon and Vectran (a strong woven fiber) on the calibration target of its SHERLOC instrument (an ultraviolet scanner that looks for minerals and carbon compounds), and Teflon and basalt glass on the target of PIXL (an X-ray instrument that reads the chemistry of rocks). It is the first measurement on Mars itself of fine dust (smaller than 2.5 micrometers, far thinner than a hair) and ultrafine dust (about 100 nanometers). Grains averaged about 2 micrometers on some swatches and only 100 to 300 nanometers on others; static electricity decides which grains stick to which material. The dust is rich in iron and sulfur, has extra phosphorus and signs of calcium sulfate, and Mars dust also carries perchlorates (salts that are toxic to people). The study, led by Scott VanBommel of Washington University in St. Louis, was published on 27 October in PNAS (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences). Quoted: Lindsay Hays, acting director of NASA's Planetary Science Division, and Katie Stack Morgan, the project scientist at JPL.
feed.evidence: official NASA release about a peer-reviewed paper; I read NASA's copy on nasa.gov, and on 29 October the JPL copy opened too; I did not open the paper itself
feed.other: This is the story @NASAMars posted about on 26 October (see the next item).

feed.who: NASA Mars 2020 team blog, "Tinga's Tale", by Margaret Deahn (Purdue University)
feed.text: Describes a target named "Tinga" at the southern border of "Idubi", an outcrop made mostly of olivine (an igneous mineral). At Tinga the lower rock is likely a breccia (rock made of broken, angular pieces, often formed by an impact), and higher dark rocks may be part of the Idubi olivine unit or breccia that was "baked" by contact with it. The team says more study is needed. The image is from sol 2009 (14 October 2026). The post is dated 26 October on NASA's site; the author's note says it was written 19 October.
feed.evidence: official NASA blog, named author (Margaret Deahn, a Purdue University Ph.D. candidate); the geology is the team's reading, not settled

feed.image_alt: Artist's impression of ESA's Mars Express spacecraft in front of Mars
feed.image_caption: An artist's impression of ESA's Mars Express at Mars (a drawing, not a photo)
feed.image_credit: ESA, CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO, via Wikimedia Commons
feed.text: Reports that ESA's Mars Express, at Mars since 2003, could support MMX when it arrives in 2027, with joint observations and imaging of the landing site. Says Mars Express's latest extension runs to 2029 and, quoting a former team member, is "definitely the last" (the same person notes the first "last ever extension" was around 2007). Says JAXA reported on 21 October that MMX's initial critical operations, including solar array deployment, were complete. Says MMX plans to collect about 10 g from Phobos, with return in 2031, and that ESA's Trace Gas Orbiter, not Mars Express, will be the main relay for the Rosalind Franklin rover.
feed.evidence: named reporter; the 2029 date comes from the article, not from ESA [unconfirmed against ESA]; ESA's June 2026 release says only that Mars Express was extended
feed.other: ESA's 11 June 2026 release lists Mars Express among missions given extensions, with no end date in the text I read.

feed.who: JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency), release "Completion of the Initial Critical Operations Phase" of MMX
feed.image_alt: Comic-style drawing of the MMX trip: launch from Tanegashima, arrival at Mars, then Phobos
feed.image_caption: Part of an ESA infographic, a drawing and not a photo: launch in October 2026, Mars in August 2027, Phobos in September 2027
feed.image_credit: ESA, CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO, via Wikimedia Commons
feed.text: JAXA says MMX finished its first, risky days in space: the solar panels unfolded, the spacecraft holds itself steady on all three axes, and the medium-gain antenna (a mid-size dish for talking to Earth) was released from its launch locks. The spacecraft is healthy. Next come checks of each system, then the long cruise to Mars. Seen 28 October (we had it only through The Register before). On 26 October JAXA's MMX blog posted a team member's account of hearing the first signal after launch; it has no new status.
feed.evidence: JAXA's own release and blog
feed.other: Dates: JAXA's MMX press kit (in Japanese, opened 28 Oct) gives fiscal years only: arrive at Mars in FY2027, leave Mars in FY2030, back at Earth in FY2031 (Japan's fiscal year runs April to March). It plans two landings on Phobos, with the small rover going down first. NASA's 8 October advisory says MMX arrives in August 2027, collects its sample no earlier than December 2028, and returns it in 2031. ESA says the landing is in 2030, so the landing date is still [unconfirmed].

feed.who: Vandi Verma, chief engineer for robotic operations, NASA JPL (Perseverance blog)
feed.where: NASA science blog, "Tracks Along the Longest Drive on Another World"
feed.text: Verma (post dated 12 October, published 21 October) says the odometer read 45.22 km (28.10 miles) on sol 2006 and explains the driving upgrades behind it: a higher tilt limit (24 degrees), smaller required belly clearance (20 cm), new braking and wheel-slip software, and an on-board position-finding tool that works like GPS on a world without it. About 200 meters short of the record on sol 1947, the team stayed to study outcrops instead of driving on. She says the team is exploring using generative AI to help plan paths.
feed.evidence: official NASA blog, named author; the AI use is described as being explored, not in use

feed.who: NASA Ames Research Center (Arezu Sarvestani), "NASA Experimental Mars Helicopter Blade Designs Target Longer Flights"
feed.image_alt: A thin, slightly curved silver metal test piece of a rotor blade on a stand, in front of a ruler marked in centimeters
feed.image_caption: The picture NASA uses for the article: a thin metal rotor-blade test piece beside a ruler. The page does not caption this picture, so I do not know which design it is
feed.text: Missed by earlier runs; seen 28 October. NASA engineers, with Imperial College London and Japan's Nagoya University, designed a thinner, sharper rotor blade for Mars's thin air, called roamx-0201. Computer studies say it could stretch a single helicopter flight from Ingenuity's 0.7 km to as much as 18.7 km while carrying instruments. Wind-tunnel tests backed up the gains. NASA says its SkyFall mission, a trio of Mars helicopters, is "scheduled for launch in 2028" and uses Ingenuity-style blades; the new design is for missions after that. The paper was published on 22 September in an American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics journal.
feed.evidence: official NASA article; SkyFall's 2028 launch is a NASA plan that Congress has not fully funded [aspirational]

feed.text: JAXA announces that MMX launched on H3 flight No. 10 at 04:41:03 Japan time on 20 October 2026 (19:41 UTC on 19 October) from the Tanegashima Space Center. The rocket flew as planned; the spacecraft separated 71 minutes 13 seconds after liftoff and was placed in its planned orbit. The release gives no Mars arrival date.
feed.evidence: JAXA's own release
feed.other: Arrival: ESA says MMX enters Mars orbit in August 2027 and orbits Phobos from September 2027; NASASpaceFlight (Justin Davenport, 19 Oct) also says August 2027. ESA says the Phobos landing is in 2030; NASASpaceFlight says the landings come no earlier than December 2028. Those two disagree, so the landing date is [unconfirmed]. JAXA's press kit, seen only in search results, gives fiscal years only.

feed.who: NASA Curiosity team blog, sols 5036-5042, by Alex Innanen (York University)
feed.text: Says a new Mars year, number 39, began at the end of September and it is now autumn in Gale crater. The team finished a drill campaign at "Basque Lakes" (including one more gas-analysis experiment by the SAM instrument) and planned to drive back toward the "Chiu Chiu" region, where it had seen crystal forms. The first high-altitude twilight clouds of the season showed up. Earth planning date was 9 October; the image is from sol 5037 (7 October 2026).
feed.evidence: official NASA blog, named author (Alex Innanen, York University); the sol-to-date arithmetic elsewhere on this page is ours

feed.text: On Starship's tenth birthday: SpaceX's Starship has not flown to Mars; this year's Mars window (the roughly 26-month period when Earth and Mars line up for a launch) is closing with no Starship Mars launch; the next window is late 2028 to early 2029. Says Starship Flight 14 on 28 September reached orbit and that Flights 15 and 16 have no confirmed dates.
feed.evidence: named reporter summarizing company statements; no new SpaceX statement quoted for dates [aspirational]
feed.other: SpaceX's own Mars page (read 27 Oct) says Starship cargo flights to the Martian surface start "no earlier than 2028" [aspirational]. I found no Elon Musk post about a Mars launch date between 13 and 27 October; the only Mars-related post I found was a 16 October post about his Roadster car, a quip and not a program statement.

feed.who: ESA, "ExoMars rover twin rehearses first drive" (first seen in our 31 Oct check)
feed.text: Before ESA's Rosalind Franklin rover can explore Mars it must drive off its landing platform, which ESA calls one of the mission's most critical moments. In a two-month test in Turin, Italy, a full-size twin rover called Amalia drove off a model of the platform more than 20 times: with a ceiling hoist carrying two-thirds of its weight to copy Mars's lower gravity, on a platform tilted 20 degrees, and with obstacles under the ramps. The platform has two pairs of ramps, front and back, and ground control will choose which way to drive off using only pictures from orbit; "once we egress, there is no way back," said Eric Zekri, ESA's ExoMars rover team leader. The rover weighs 300 kg on Earth; the 3-meter aluminum ramps were made by the Polish company Astronika, and the tests were run by Thales Alenia Space (the main contractor) at ALTEC. ESA says the rover's journey on the Martian surface begins in 2030.
feed.evidence: ESA's own story; the test photos are Thales Alenia Space pictures under ESA's standard license, so none is shown here. The 2030 landing year is ESA's own statement, matching NASA's April slides (launch 2028) [no independent check of the date]
feed.other: ESA's October video round-up also mentions this test and a Mars Express finding about a giant Martian cloud.

feed.who: NASA science editorial team, "NASA's Perseverance Sets Off-World Record for Total Distance Driven"
feed.text: NASA says Perseverance passed the record for total distance driven on another world, held by NASA's Opportunity rover: 45.22 km (28.10 miles) on sol 2006 (11 October 2026) against Opportunity's 45.16 km (28.06 miles); that day's drive was 91.31 meters. It took Perseverance about five and a half years; Opportunity took almost 15. NASA also says the mission's first extension began in October and runs to roughly the end of 2028, and that the rover is heading toward "Idubi" and then south toward a block of uplifted ancient crust called Rainbow Falls. NASA says Perseverance has collected 29 rock and regolith samples (CNN counts 33 tubes, which also includes dust and air samples).
feed.evidence: official NASA blog

feed.who: Ashley Strickland, CNN
feed.text: Reports that Mars Sample Return was cancelled with no clear alternative. Quotes a July NASA statement: NASA is "exploring a range of potential return options" that could be simpler and cheaper, "including possible commercial or international contributions". Quotes NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman (30 August): "There's no question we're going to go get samples", robot or astronaut, with no time frame. Says Perseverance has filled 33 tubes (NASA's own count of rock and regolith samples is 29), and that China's Tianwen-3 aims to return its own samples in 2031.
feed.evidence: named reporter; NASA statement and Isaacman quotes as printed; Lockheed Martin's under-$3 billion return concept (by 2037) is a company claim [aspirational]
feed.other: Where the budget papers stand on Mars Sample Return: NASA's 2026 request said it "plans to terminate" the program. For 2027, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) says the request "reiterates the cancellation", while CNN says the request does not mention it at all; the two read the document differently. The 2026 spending law gave $110 million for Mars Future Missions (NASA slides); the Planetary Society, an advocacy group, says that money was meant to buy down technical risk for a restructured sample return, and that the House committee bill for 2027 is "silent" on it.

feed.text: Reports that the House committee's bill for 2027 keeps NASA flat at $24.4 billion, with Planetary Science at $2.5 billion and Mars Exploration at $300 million (the group's tables). The group says the bill is "silent" on Mars Sample Return. As far as I read, the full House has not passed it. Congress, not the White House request, sets the final amounts. Next: midterm elections on 3 November; the stopgap law runs out on 11 December.

feed.who: American Astronomical Society (AAS), summary of NASA's 2027 budget request
feed.kind: professional society (secondary summary of a government document)
feed.text: White House request for 2027: NASA $18.829 billion, 23% below the $24.438 billion enacted for 2026; Planetary Science $1.876 billion (down 26%); Mars Exploration $248.3 million; Perseverance operations $38.0 million, down from $87.5 million in the 2024 plan (AAS says NASA is "reassessing objectives for the mission"); Mars Future Missions $110 million. AAS reads Mars Odyssey, the U.S. part of Mars Express and the U.S. contribution to ESA's Rosalind Franklin rover as missions the request does not mention, meaning proposed endings carried over from the 2026 request; the House committee report protects some other science missions, and I did not confirm it names these three.
feed.evidence: society's summary of NASA's own document; figures as printed; I did not open the request itself

board.s: Working. Finished drilling at Basque Lakes (42nd drill hole) and is preparing to drill at "Nazca", a block with possible crystal shapes (NASA blog, 28 Oct). Climbing Mount Sharp; 1 km of elevation gain reached 26 Aug 2026. FY2027 request keeps it funded at $38.0M. NASA's raw-image feed shows new pictures through sol 5059 (30 Oct).

Working. World-record 45.22 km driven by sol 2006 (11 Oct); NASA's traverse file shows 45.25 km by sol 2022 (28 Oct). Exploring Lac de Charmes, outside Jezero's western rim, near the Idubi outcrop. Drilled a new sample, "Singita", on 24 Oct, its first in more than a year (Planetary Society, from the project scientist's talk; no NASA story yet). NASA counted 29 rock and regolith samples before that, none returned; first mission extension began in October, to about end of 2028. FY2027 request would cut operations from $87.5M (2024) to $38.0M. New on 26 Oct: NASA published its dust study from swatches of spacesuit material the rover carries.
board.d: 31 Oct 2026 (raw images to sol 2024; traverse file sol 2022; blog 26 Oct)

At Mars since 2003 (The Register). ESA lists it among missions extended in June 2026 (no end date in the text). The Register (22 Oct) says the latest extension runs to 2029 and calls it the last [secondary source; not confirmed on an ESA page]. The course had said funding was secure only to end of 2026, with 2029 proposed.

Operating. The UAE Space Agency announced on 17 Feb 2026 that the mission is extended, through 2028. Course: more than 10 terabytes of data returned (The National; WAM; not re-checked for the figure).

Operating. CNSA said in April 2026 it had kept surveying Mars (reported via Xinhua on marsprogress.com). Amateur tracker Daniel Estévez saw a radio gap in Dec 2025, the signal return, and a safe-mode event on 2 Aug 2026 [amateur sourced; China has said little].

Launched 20 Oct 2026 (04:41 Japan time). Healthy; first critical operations done (solar panels out, steady pointing, antenna released), JAXA 21 Oct; now checking its systems before the cruise. CNES woke the Idefix rover on board for a test on 30 Oct, which went well; next wake-up in a month (CNES on X). Reaches Mars: August 2027 per ESA, NASA and NASASpaceFlight; JAXA's press kit says fiscal year 2027. Phobos sample: no earlier than December 2028 per NASA and NASASpaceFlight, 2030 per ESA [unconfirmed]. Leaves Mars FY2030; samples back on Earth in 2031 (JAXA press kit, NASA, ESA).

perseverance.area: "Lac de Charmes", outside the western rim of Jezero crater, near "Idubi", an olivine-rich outcrop; the rover drilled the "Singita" sample here on 24 October and plans to try for two more (Planetary Society).
perseverance.est_note: NASA's raw-image feed lists images from sol 2024 taken on 30 October 2026 (Mastcam-Z, Navcam and SuperCam pictures; the feed shows no new drive since sol 2022); 31 October is about one sol later (our own arithmetic, one sol is about 1.0275 Earth days)
perseverance.note: The distance comes from NASA's public traverse file (a list of the rover's stopping points), because no NASA blog gives a newer figure. That file lags and does not update every day. Its newest point is sol 2022 (28 Oct): 45,245.7 meters in total (45.25 km, 28.11 miles), after a 22-meter drive. The record figure NASA announced was 45.22 km for sol 2006 (11 Oct). If NASA's blog is newer, the daily check uses the blog's numbers.

curiosity.t: Latest NASA blog: sols 5043 to 5049, posted 28 October 2026 by Lucy Lim (NASA Goddard). After Basque Lakes the rover went back near "Chiu Chiu" and is preparing to drill "Nazca", a block packed with disc- and needle-shaped possible crystals. It also planned night pictures of Phobos to study high, thin clouds; the twilight cloud season is starting. The plan is from 16 October, so the drilling may already have happened.
The previous blog (sols 5036 to 5042, 19 October, Alex Innanen): drill campaign at "Basque Lakes" finished; it is autumn in Gale crater; a new Mars year (number 39) began at the end of September.

NASA's raw-image feed has pictures through sol 5059, taken on 30 October 2026, so 31 October is about sol 5060 (our own arithmetic). NASA's pages that I opened give no odometer for 30 October, so none is shown here.
Climbing Mount Sharp, the mound in Gale crater: 1 kilometer of elevation gain reached on 26 August 2026, per NASA's mission page, which also counts 42 drill holes.

Distance: NASA's 12 October record release says Curiosity has driven more than 38.07 km (23.65 miles). Money: the FY2027 request puts Curiosity (the Mars Science Laboratory line) at $38.0M, from $40.0M in the 2024 plan (AAS summary of NASA's request); Congress has not set the final 2027 number.

plans.t: Says Starship cargo flights to the Martian surface start no earlier than 2028 and prices cargo at $100 million per metric ton. In February 2026 Elon Musk said the company would for now give priority to a city on the Moon (The Guardian, as cited in the course; I did not open it). Flight 14 reached orbit on 28 September (Space.com).

plans.t: NASA's April slides say a nuclear-electric spacecraft, SR-1 Freedom, targets Mars in 2028 and would release "SkyFall" helicopters (a NASA article of 20 Oct says SkyFall is "scheduled for launch in 2028"). The House committee bill supports it, and the Planetary Society repeats NASA's plan to fly it "before the end of 2028". Funding is not final.
plans.label: aspirational

plans.t: Launch about 2028, samples back about 2031. Eight candidate landing zones; final site expected by end of 2026; at the engineering prototype stage (Xinhua, April and September 2026). Two launches, one lander with a drill and a helicopter (CNN, citing the mission team's 2025 paper). A rumor on X (27 Oct) says the lander may slip two years, pushing samples to about 2033 [unconfirmed; China has said nothing].
plans.label: aspirational

ESA's 12 October story says the rover's journey on the surface begins in 2030 (ESA's own date; no exact month given). The 2027 U.S. budget request does not mention the U.S. contribution.

plans.t: A lander-and-orbiter follow-up to India's first Mars mission. The only on-record statement I opened: Nilesh Desai, a director at ISRO, told ANI on 8 October 2025 that work has begun and that it "will be completed by 2028-2030", and that the trip takes 10 months. No official launch date or approved budget found [unconfirmed].

plans.t: No agency has an approved, funded, dated crewed mission to Mars as of 31 October 2026 that I could find. NASA calls Mars a "horizon goal" after the Moon (course, citing NASA release 26-025, which I did not open). Treat any crewed-Mars date, from SpaceX or anyone, as a goal.

glossary: one Martian day, about 24 hours 39 minutes. Rovers count their days in sols from landing.
the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter, an instrument that measured Mars's heights by laser; used for the course's maps.
in-situ resource use: making water, air or fuel from what is already on Mars instead of bringing it.
a company challenges a federal contract award at the Government Accountability Office, which must decide within about 100 days.
continuing resolution: a stopgap law that keeps agencies funded at last year's level while Congress finishes the new budget.
Japan's government year runs from April to March, so "fiscal year 2027" means April 2027 to March 2028.
the roughly 26-month period when Earth and Mars line up well for a launch.
